chunks: "Health has a few dimensions, and I'd check them in this order. First, capacity.
I do a full charge, rest, and a controlled discharge at a low rate to the cutoff, integrating current, and compare to the rated value.
State of health is capacity now over rated capacity, and a common end-of-life line is about 80 percent. Second, internal resistance.
A fresh 2 amp-hour cell might be 50 milliohms, and as it ages it climbs.
I measure it with a DC pulse: take the rested voltage, apply a known current step, and the voltage change over the current is the resistance.
A quick AC check at 1 kilohertz with an IR meter also works, though it captures mostly the ohmic part.
Resistance matters because it limits peak power and creates heat, and it can age out of spec even when capacity still looks fine.
Third, I check self-discharge and imbalance: a cell that loses voltage faster than its siblings may have an internal short.
In a pack, compare the cells' voltage and resistance, since the weakest one decides.
Fourth, I look at physical signs: swelling, warm spots, odd smell, voltage that sags under a normal load. A swollen cell is retired regardless of its numbers.
In a product, the fuel gauge does this continuously by tracking learned capacity and resistance, plus cycle count and temperature history, and reports state of health."
